1.title: Know words, readers and the job of copy
1.intro: Copy is writing that helps a reader take one clear step. Start with the basic words and the people you write for.
pts: Learn the terms: headline, body, call to action, benefit, feature, tone, brief.
A feature is what a thing has. A benefit is what the reader gains from it.
Name one reader in one line: who they are, what they want, what worries them.
Read five ads or web pages and mark the headline, the benefit and the call to action.
1.ex: Feature: 'The mug keeps drinks hot for six hours.' Benefit: 'Your coffee is still hot when the meeting ends.' Call to action: 'Order today.'
1.act: Pick five pieces of copy and mark headline, benefit and call to action on each. Write a one-line reader profile.
1.std: Task: label the parts of five pieces of copy. Condition: with a printed or saved sample and no help. Standard: all parts labelled correctly and the reader profile fits one line.

2.title: Explain how a copy job runs from brief to delivery
2.intro: A job has steps. If you can name them, you can plan your time and avoid surprises.
pts: The steps are brief, research, outline, draft, edit, review, final files.
A brief says who the reader is, the goal, the tone, the length, the deadline and the one action wanted.
Ask questions before you write; a short call saves a rewrite.
Agree how many rounds of changes are included.
2.ex: A client asks for a web page. You ask: Who buys? What do they do now? What action do you want? What can we not say? Then you write an outline for approval.
2.act: Write a one-page brief form with ten questions and test it on a friend who runs a small shop.
2.std: Task: complete a brief for a real or pretend client. Condition: in one conversation of 30 minutes. Standard: the brief states reader, goal, action, tone, length, deadline and number of change rounds.

3.title: Write a clear short piece to a standard
3.intro: Now you apply the basics. Write short pieces that are clear, true and easy to scan.
pts: Use short words and short sentences. Put the main point first.
Write three headline options and pick the one that is clear before it is clever.
Use real facts the client can prove. Do not make claims you cannot support.
Read aloud and cut every word that does nothing.
3.ex: Before: 'We offer a wide range of premium solutions.' After: 'We fix leaking taps the same day. Call before 3 p.m.' The second names the service, the speed and the step.
3.act: Write a 150-word product page and three headlines. Edit it twice and keep both drafts.
3.std: Task: write a 150-word page. Condition: from a written brief, within two hours. Standard: one action only, every claim checkable, no spelling errors, and the second draft is shorter and clearer than the first.

4.title: Follow Canadian rules for advertising and messages
4.intro: Canada has rules for honest advertising, email and language. Learn which ones touch your copy.
pts: Advertising must not be false or misleading. A price, a discount or a result must be true and clear.
Commercial email and text messages need consent, a clear sender name and a working way to unsubscribe. Check the current anti-spam rules.
In Quebec, commercial advertising generally needs French. Check the current language rules with the provincial office.
Personal information you use in copy is covered by privacy law. Ask before using a customer name or story.
4.ex: A client wants 'Best in Canada'. You ask for proof. They have none, so you write 'Loved by 200 local families' only after they show you the count.
4.act: Make a table of rule, who enforces it, what you must do, and where you checked, for ten claims you often write.
4.std: Task: build a claims and rules table. Condition: using official public pages. Standard: each row has a dated source; no rule is guessed; unclear cases say 'check the current rule with the local authority'.

5.title: Price your work and check it pays
5.intro: You are paid for results and time. Work out your cost per hour and what a project must earn.
pts: Time includes research, calls, drafting, edits and admin, not just typing.
Hourly cost = yearly costs and the pay you need, divided by hours you can really bill.
Compare per-hour, per-page and per-project pricing; use a project price only when the scope is clear.
Collect sales tax once registered; check the small-supplier limit with the tax agency.
5.ex: A page takes 4 hours at 55 USD an hour: 220 USD. If your tools cost 5 USD for the job, margin is 215 USD. Teaching figures only.
5.act: Time three pieces from start to finish. Compute your real hours per piece and set a price for each.
5.std: Task: price three projects. Condition: from your own time log and a simple spreadsheet. Standard: hours, rate and total shown; a mentor can follow every number.

6.title: Find clients and show proof
6.intro: Clients buy from writers they trust. Build a small portfolio and a steady way to be found.
pts: Make three samples that match the kind of client you want, with the brief shown beside each.
Get written permission before showing client work.
Reach out to ten local businesses with one specific idea each, not a general pitch.
Keep a simple list: contact, date, reply, next step.
6.ex: You email a bakery: 'Your online order page has no call to action. Here is a 60-word rewrite.' You attach it and ask for a 15-minute call.
6.act: Send ten tailored messages in two weeks and log the replies.
6.std: Task: run a two-week outreach. Condition: using only legal, consent-based contact. Standard: ten messages sent with consent rules met, replies logged, one lesson written.

7.title: Protect ownership, privacy and quality
7.intro: A professional writer is careful with rights, client secrets and facts.
pts: Write down who owns the copy and what the client may do with it. Check with a legal adviser for large deals.
Do not copy other people's writing or images; use your own words or licensed material.
Keep client files safe: strong passwords, backups, access only for those who need it.
Fact-check names, prices, dates and quotes before delivery.
7.ex: Your contract says: 'The client owns the final copy once paid in full. The writer may show it in a portfolio unless the client objects.'
7.act: Write a one-page agreement template and a delivery checklist for facts, spelling, links and file formats.
7.std: Task: produce a template and checklist. Condition: reviewed by a mentor. Standard: scope, fees, rounds, rights, payment date and privacy are all stated in plain words.

8.title: Run your practice for real and grow it
8.intro: Now you run it: take real jobs, measure them and decide how to grow.
pts: Set a 60-day pilot goal, such as three paid clients and one repeat job.
Each week record hours, income, late payments and client feedback.
Ask each client for a short review and one thing to improve.
At the end choose: stop, change or grow, and write a 12-month plan.
8.ex: After 60 days: 3 clients, 22 hours, 1,100 USD billed, one client came back. You decide to raise the rate and stop low-fee work.
8.act: Run the pilot, keep the weekly log and present a 12-month plan to a panel of three.
8.std: Task: run a 60-day practice pilot. Condition: real clients and paid or agreed work. Standard: the log is complete, the decision uses numbers, and a panel can repeat your plan.

quiz: What is the difference between a feature and a benefit?
A feature is what a thing has; a benefit is what the reader gains.
What should a good brief state?
Reader, goal, action wanted, tone, length, deadline and change rounds.
Why write a headline three ways?
To pick the one that is clearest, not just clever.
What must be true of every claim in your copy?
It can be proved and is not misleading.
What do commercial emails and texts need in Canada?
Consent, a clear sender and a working way to unsubscribe.
How do you find your real hourly cost?
Yearly costs plus needed pay, divided by hours you can really bill.
Why get permission before showing client work?
The work belongs to the client unless the agreement says otherwise.
What should a simple agreement list?
Scope, fees, rounds of changes, rights, payment date and privacy.
What do you check before delivering copy?
Facts, names, prices, spelling, links and file formats.
What do you do when you do not know a rule?
Check the current rule with the local authority and keep the answer in writing.
